summary_plain: This experiment burned gaseous fuels like methane, ethylene, and propane in co-flowing air inside the microgravity science glovebox aboard the International Space Station. By removing gravity-driven buoyancy, researchers studied laminar smoke points and soot formation without gravity interference. Understanding how and when flames begin to emit soot helps improve fire safety and spacecraft environmental controls.
summary_expert: The Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE) investigated non-buoyant laminar jet diffusion flames aboard the International Space Station inside the Microgravity Science Glovebox. The test matrix utilized burner diameters of 0.41 mm, 0.76 mm, and 1.6 mm, co-flow velocities ranging from 5.4 cm/s to 65 cm/s, and fuels including ethylene, propane, propylene, and mixtures of 50 and 75 percent propylene by volume in nitrogen. Over the course of the mission phases, hundreds of test points were completed to examine smoke point behavior, luminous flame lengths, and residence time effects. Results demonstrated that increasing co-flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths, while smaller burners exhibit longer smoke points for co-flowing flames.

key_findings.text: During Increment 18 SPICE conducted 108 test points completing its nominal test matrix, and during Increments 19/20 SPICE conducted 155 additional test points.
Increasing co-flow velocity decreases luminous flame lengths, but moves smoke points to higher fuel flow rates and longer luminous flame lengths.
Smaller burners have longer smoke points for coflowing flames.
